newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine government brushes off Dec 26 strike.
newsitem.headline: Argentine government brushes off Dec 26 strike.

text.p: Argentina's government Monday remained undettered in its policy to reform the labor market to alleviate unemployment, dismissing unions' decision to strike as a mere "tourist" stoppage.

President Carlos Menem brushed aside the 24-hour strike planned for Thursday to protest three decrees on labor reform he signed last week. He said the decrees are aimed at "alleviating unemployment" and will benefit small companies.
Echoing statements in response to the last general strike Sept 26, Menem said this was just another excuse to give workers more time off during Christmas.
"Of course on the 24th it's Christmas and then comes the strike. That is to say, it is a tourist strike," Menem said.
Argentina's main CGT union federation decided late Friday to stage its third general strike this year, responding to labor market reforms that are seen reducing worker's rights.
The decrees signed by Menem late Wednesday came after weeks of negotiations with the unions ended in stalemate.

The moves allow workers to decide which union health plan they sign up to and permit smaller firms to bypass national unions in collective wage talks with workers. Also, employers will now be able to appeal to the government if they want to negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis.

"We are convinced that all Argentine workers will join us," said Rodolfo Daer, the CGT chief. Daer said the CGT would also challenge the labor decrees in court but stopped short of calling for public protests on the strike day as well.
Labor Minister Armando Caro Figueroa said the CGT has staged other strikes "without any vindication and afterwards they came back to negotiate."

The CGT has already staged general strikes in August and September, protesting unemployment, austerity measures and the labor reforms. The 36-hour strike in September was the biggest challenge yet to Menem's free-market reforms but he dismissed it as a "complete failure."
The CGT has said it will meet again Dec 30 to discuss its plan of action after the strike to put further pressure on the government's labor market reform plans.
However, the government is dead set on deepening the reforms, be it through presidential decrees to bypass reluctant lawmakers or otherwise.

Even before the strike was announced, Economy Ministry Roque Fernandez said most of the pending labor market reforms would be introduced by decree. He said decrees were necessary because delays in labor reforms could risk World Bank credits.

Economists argue that the increased flexibility of labor reforms are absolutely necessary to reduce large employer costs in hiring and firing Argentine workers. Those costs are important obstacles to firms employing more workers.
The government says the reforms are key to cut stubbornly high unemployment, currently at 17.3 percent.
